title: Which check is stronger?

job.text: You want the AI to flag refunds over $100 in a list. Two non-vacuous check requests are offered. Pick the stronger one — the one that's right on every row.

naivePrompt: Check that it mentions a dollar amount.
basePrompt: Check that it mentions a dollar amount.

text.plain: Flag any line that mentions a dollar amount.
Flag every line where the amount is over $100, and flag none that are $100 or under.

rules.claim: Flags the 3 over $100, leaves the 2 under alone.
rules.feedback: Right in both directions. It catches every refund over $100 and leaves the small ones alone. That's a two-sided check.
rules.lesson: A strong check is correct on good and bad cases.

output.source: a check that's right on every row

rules.claim: Flags all 5 lines, including the $40 one.
rules.feedback: False green on the $40 row. "Mentions a dollar amount" is true of a $40 line — so it flags one it shouldn't. Saying yes too often is as broken as saying no too rarely.
rules.lesson: A check must say no when it should, too.

output.source: a check that says yes too often

rules.feedback: Pick a check. One of these flags the $40 row it shouldn't; the other is right on every row. Run the test-bench to see which is which.
rules.lesson: A strong check is right on good and bad cases alike.

output.source: pick one and run the bench

hints.nudge: Does it only say yes when it should — and no when it shouldn't?
hints.gap: Watch the $40 row: "mentions a dollar amount" flags it, but $40 isn't over $100.
hints.moves: Pick Flags only amounts over $100 — it's the one that's right on every row. Leave "flags any dollar amount" off.

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: "check it mentions a dollar amount" → flags a $40 line it shouldn't.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: "flag over $100, flag none under" → correct on every row.

template.plain: Write a check that flags X and does NOT flag not-X. Show me it on an example of each — one that should be flagged and one that shouldn't.
template.tech: Write a check where flagged == (condition). Run it on a positive example and a borderline negative example and show both verdicts.

notes: ChatGPT: make it run both examples; a check that flags the wrong one is too loose.
Copilot in Excel: the check column should be TRUE on the over rows and FALSE on the under rows — eyeball both.
A chat AI that can't run code: ask it for a borderline example and whether the check fires — that reveals the threshold. Never accept "I checked, it's fine."
